extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of Roman history; historians and writers modelling classical historiographical style
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and exemplars for composing narrative histories of Rome—choices about what to record, how to report facts, and the historian's moral purpose. Useful for historians or creative writers aiming to emulate classical historiography.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty of the historian: record virtue and vice
rubrics_metrics.description: "This I conceive to be the principal duty of an historian, that he suppress no instance of virtue; and that by the dread of future infamy and the censures of posterity, men may be deterred from detestable actions and prostitute speeches."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The historian should not omit examples of virtue or of notorious wrongdoing; recording both serves a moral purpose — to praise good conduct and deter future vice by the shame of posterity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impartial presentation of facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Tiberius wrote to the Senate "and at once acquainted them with its rise and conclusion, neither aggravating facts nor lessening them".
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report events accurately and without rhetorical exaggeration or minimisation. Present the rise and conclusion of affairs candidly rather than embellishing or downplaying facts to serve a partisan purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selectivity: include votes or details only when notable
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is no part of my purpose to trace all the votes of particular men, unless they are memorable for integrity, or for notorious infamy."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be selective in minutiae: do not exhaustively list routine votes or petty actions. Include specific votes, speeches, or procedural details only when they are striking for virtue or infamy, or otherwise materially illuminate character or consequence.
